text: nature plants The BRUTUS iron sensor and E3 ligase facilitates soybean root nodulation by monoubiquitination of NSP1 1,3 1, Zhijuan Wang & Xia Li Legumes form root nodules with symbiotic nitrogen-fixing rhizobacteria, which require ample iron to ensure symbiosis establishment and efficient nitrogen fixation. The functions and mechanisms of iron in nitrogen-fixing nodules are well established. However, the role of iron and the mechanisms by which legumes sense iron and incorporate this cue into nodulation signalling pathways remain unclear. Here we show that iron is a key driver of nodulation because symbiotic nodules cannot form without iron, even under conditions of sufficient light and low nitrogen. We further identify an iron optimum for soybean nodulation and the iron sensor BRUTUS A (BTSa) which acts as a hub for integrating iron and nodulation cues. BTSa is induced by rhizobia, binds to and is stabilized by iron. In turn, BTSa stabilizes and enhances the transcriptional activation activity of pro-nodulation transcription factor NSP1a by monoubiquitination from its RING domain and consequently activates nodulation signalling. Monoubiquitination of NSP1 by BTS is conserved in legumes to trigger nodulation under iron sufficiency. Thus, iron status is an essential cue to trigger nodulation and BTSa integrates cues from rhizobial infection and iron status to orchestrate Symbiotic nitrogen fixation between legume plants and nitrogen-fixing rhizobacteria is the largest potential natural source of new nitrogen in the biosphere, with implications for global primary production, carbon sequestration and element cycling1–4.

text: Under low-nitrogen conditions, legumes release flavonoid compounds to induce rhizobia to produce and secrete lipochitooligosaccharides (LCOs), known as nodulation (Nod) factors. Nod factors are sensed on the plasma membrane of root-hair cells by host Nod-factor receptors5–10. The perception of Nod factors by the LysM receptor kinase complexes triggers the nodulation signalling cascade by inducing nuclear calcium spiking, decoding of the calcium signals and activating a series of transcription factors, including NODULATION SIGNALLING PATHWAY 1/2 (NSP1/2) and its host responses towards establishing symbiotic nitrogen fixation. downstream nodulation-essential gene NODULE INCEPTION (NIN), which controls all known nodulation procecsses11–19. Rhizobia then infect and colonize root cells to form root nodules wherein rhizobial nitrogenases reduce dinitrogen to ammonia to provide the host plant with sufficient nitrogen, in exchange for organic molecules from photosynthesis20,21. The formation and maintenance of nodule functions require substantial resources, and host plants tightly control nodule numbers through a root–shoot long-distance negative regulatory system called autoregulation of nodulation (AON)22–29. However, nodule formation and function are also influenced by environmental factors, such as light and nutrients, which provide carbon and essential elements for symbiotic nitrogen fixation1,30–37.

text: Wuhan, China. 595 Iron (Fe) is a vital micronutrient for all forms of life. Despite being the second-most-abundant metal element on our planet, iron mainly exists in the highly insoluble ferric form in most habitats, making it difficult for bacteria and plants to absorb and use directly38. Iron is a key component or cofactor of various proteins or enzymes in plant cells and plays pivotal roles in diverse processes, such as respiration, photosynthesis and metabolism of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species39. In legumes, both nitrogenase in nitrogen-fixing bacteria and leghaemoglobin in infected nodule cells are iron-containing proteins; thus iron levels directly regulate nitrogenase activity, thereby influencing the efficiency of symbiotic nitrogen fixation40,41. While the link between symbiotic nitrogen fixation in root nodules and iron has been well documented in legumes, the roles and mechanisms of iron during the early stages of nodulation are still not fully understood. Limited research has suggested that certain legumes, such as Lupinus angustifolius, do not form nodules in iron-deficient environments, highlighting the essential role of iron in rhizobia–host interaction, infection and nodule development42–44. Inadequate iron levels have been shown to reduce nodule formation in different legume species, such as soybean (Glycine max)36,45. The effects of varying concentrations of iron on nodulation and the optimal iron requirement for nodulation have not been comprehensively studied yet.

text: To cope with fluctuations in environmental iron levels, plants have evolved mechanisms to sense iron status and modulate the expression of genes involved in iron absorption and transport. This is achieved via a transcriptional regulatory network consisting of a set of transcription factors (TFs)46. In Arabidopsis, under iron deficiency, FER-LIKE IRON-DEFICIENCY-INDUCED TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR 1 (FIT1) interacts with Ib-subgroup bHLH TFs (bHLH38/39/100/101) to regulate iron uptake-related genes such as FERRIC REDUCTASE-OXIDASE 2 (FRO2) and IRON-REGULATED TRANSPORTER 1 (IRT1)47–50. The expression of FIT and Ib-bHLH TFs is induced by upstream IVb-subgroup bHLH TFs (bHLH121/URI) and IVc-subgroup bHLH TFs (for example, bHLH105/ ILR3 and bHLH115)51–54. bHLH121/URI is phosphorylated and interacts with subgroup-IVc bHLH TFs to induce Ib-bHLH TFs, POPEYE (PYE), BRUTUS (BTS) and BRUTUS-LIKE (BTSL), to activate the iron-deficiency response53,54. BTS/BTSL are E3 ligases that contain Fe-binding haemerythrin (HHE) domains in the N terminus, a CHY zinc-finger domain and a RING domain in the C terminus55,56. When sufficient iron is available, BTS and BTSL bind to iron and interact with and ubiquitinate target proteins, including IVc bHLH TFs, bHLH121/URI and FIT, leading to their proteasomal degradation, thereby turning off the Fe-deficiency response53,54,56–58. In addition, iron-deficiency-induced IRON MAN (IMA) peptides compete with bHLH105/bHLH115 to interact with BTS, preventing the degradation of these TFs by BTS and thereby triggering the response to iron deficiency59. Thus, BTS proteins function as potential iron sensors, playing an indispensable role in maintaining iron homeostasis during plant growth and development60.

Our goal is to determine the role of iron in nodule initiation and uncover the molecular mechanism exploited by soybean to monitor external iron levels, which guarantees the formation of nodules under favourable iron conditions.

text: To determine the role of iron in soybean nodulation, we initially investigated its effect on nodulation. We inoculated the soybean reference cultivar Williams 82 (Wm82) with Bradyrhizobium diazoefficiens USDA110 rhizobia in a hydroponic growth setup with iron (Fe–EDTA) concentrations of 0, 0.4, 40 and 400 µM under low-nitrogen and sufficient light conditions. Plants formed the highest number of nodules at 40 µM iron, and almost no nodules at 0 and 400 µM iron. Consistently, infection number and primordia number were dramatically decreased under 0 and 400 µM iron (Extended Data Fig. 1a–f). To ascertain the optimal iron concentration for nodulation, we then conducted a comprehensive assessment of iron concentration, encompassing 0, 0.4, 20, 40, 80 and 160 µM, to evaluate their effects on nodulation (Extended Data Fig. 1g–n). The number of infection threads, nodule primordia, nodules and nitrogenase activity all increased up to and peaked at 40 μM but dramatically decreased at 80 μM Fe (Fig. 1a–g). Nodules barely formed at 160 μM Fe, although a few infection threads and primordia were observed (Fig. 1a–g). Our results indicate that iron is essential for soybean nodulation, with 40 μM being an optimal iron concentration, at least under this setup. Excess iron led to accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in roots (Extended Data Fig. 1h–j), potentially causing molecular damage and cell toxicity that disrupt nodulation. This aligns with previous findings on increased ROS and cytotoxicity induced by excess iron via the Fenton reaction in plant cells66.

text: NSP1a is a transcriptional activator of NIN1a in soybean nodulation11,14. Because NSP1a messenger RNA level upon inoculation was apparently unresponsive to iron supply (Extended Data Fig. 1k), we hypothesized that iron limitation reduces the transcriptional activity of NSP1a on the NIN1a promoter. To test this, we first analysed whether different iron regimes affect NSP1a stability by expressing a MYC-tagged NSP1a fusion protein from the constitutive and ubiquitous UBI1 promoter (UBIpro:NSP1a–4×MYC) in transgenic soybean hairy roots grown under normal (10 μM Fe citrate) or iron-deficient (200 μM AA-DP/2,2′-bipyridine) conditions36. NSP1a–4×MYC abundance was downregulated under iron-deficient conditions despite its transcript remaining stable between iron conditions (Fig. 2a,b), suggesting that iron promotes NSP1a accumulation. To confirm this, we assayed native NSP1 abundance in root extracts from plants treated with 10 μM Fe citrate or 200 μM AA-DP using NSP1 native antibody (specificity of antibody is shown in Extended Data Fig. 2a) and detected a downregulation of NSP1 under iron deficiency (Fig. 2c), confirming that iron can stabilize NSP1a in planta. Next, we examined the influence of iron on NSP1a–4×MYC enrichment at the NIN1a promoter by chromatin immunoprecipitation–quantitative polymerase chain reaction (ChIP–qPCR). Strong enrichment was observed in the –1,748 bp and –2,183 bp region of the NIN1a promoter in plants grown under normal conditions (Fig. 2d), consistent with a previous report67. NSP1a–4×MYC association at the NIN1a promoter was sharply reduced under iron deficiency (Fig. 2d), in agreement with NIN1a downregulation under iron limitation (Fig. 1h). To further elucidate the function of NSP1a under limited-iron conditions, we generated an nsp1a knockout mutant (Extended Data Fig. 2b–d) and characterized nodulation (Fig. 2e–g). text: The pronounced nodulation phenotype of nsp1a-1 under low-iron conditions suggests that NSP1a functions to integrate iron availability with nodulation-signalling pathways. To identify putative iron-signalling components, we performed a yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) assay to capture NSP1a-interacting proteins (Supplementary Table 1). Among the detected candidates, Glyma.05g237500 contains metal-ion-binding and DNA-binding domains and is predicted to be an E3 ubiquitin ligase, which is conserved in plants (Extended Data Fig. 3a). Its Arabidopsis orthologue BRUTUS (AtBTS) is an iron sensor that negatively regulates responses to iron deficiency57. We therefore assigned Glyma.05g237500 as BTSa on the basis of its phylogenetic relationship with AtBTS (Extended Data Fig. 3a). This led us to wonder whether BTSa potentially integrates iron and nodulation cues in soybean. To test this, we first validated the NSP1a–BTSa interaction. Full-length BTSa can interact with NSP1a in a yeast two-hybrid assay (Fig. 3a). This interaction occurs in planta in the nucleus and BTSa– 3×HA could be co-immunoprecipitated with NSP1a–GFP (Fig. 3b,c), thus confirming that BTSa is indeed an NSP1a-interacting partner. To dissect which domain(s) mediate(s) the interaction of BTSa with NSP1a, we split BTSa into an N-terminal fragment (BTSa-NTer) that includes its three haemerythrin (HHE) cation-binding domains, and a C-terminal fragment (BTSa-CTer) containing a CHY-type zinc-finger domain, a Rubredoxin-type fold and RING zinc-finger domain (Fig. 3d). In yeast, BTSa-CTer, but not BTSa-NTer, could interact with NSP1a (Fig. 3a), indicating the CHY-type/ RING zinc-finger-containing domains are sufficient for this interaction.

text: 599 Phylogenetic analyses indicate that soybean has four paralogous BTS proteins, of which BTSa and BTSb are highly homologous with 97.2% sequence similarity (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). Yeast two-hybrid assay showed that BTSb can also interact with NSP1a through its C terminus (Extended Data Fig. 3c). Together, these data suggest that both BTSa and BTSb can physically interact with NSP1a and may function in soybean nodulation.

text: To investigate the function of BTSa and BTSb in soybean nodulation, we first assayed their expression upon inoculation with rhizobia. Both BTSa and BTSb are induced by rhizobia and are highly expressed in nodules (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). BTSapro:GUS activity was restricted to the vasculature of uninoculated roots and was highly induced in whole rhizobia-infected roots (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 4c). BTSapro:GUS was highly expressed in the cortex and vascular bundles as the nodules developed and matured (Extended Data Fig. 4d). To test whether BTSa abundance is responsive to rhizobia, we transformed UBIpro:BTSa–4×MYC into hairy roots with or without rhizobial inoculation. BTSa–4×MYC was more strongly expressed in inoculated roots vs uninoculated controls (Fig. 3g), while transgene BTSa transcripts were comparable between inoculated and uninoculated hairy roots (Fig. 3h). These results suggest that BTSa expression is responsive to rhizobia at both the transcript and protein levels. We next generated two independent btsa btsb double-knockout mutants (assigned btsa btsb-1 and btsa btsb-2) by clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats–CRISPR associated 9 (CRISPR–Cas9) and evaluated their nodulation performance. Both mutant alleles have premature stop codons, express truncated BTSa and BTSb proteins containing partial HHE domains, and show no evidence of off-target edits to the corresponding target sites for BTSc and BTSd (Extended Data Fig. 4e–g). The number of infection threads, nodule primordia and nodules in both btsa btsb double mutants was markedly lower than in wild-type (WT) Wm82 controls (Fig. 3i–n), suggesting a positive role in soybean nodulation. Consistent with the impaired-nodulation phenotypes, NIN1a induction by rhizobia in the wild type was strongly attenuated in the btsa btsb-1 mutant (Fig. 3o). Taken together, these data suggest that BTSa and BTSb are required for nodulation by enhancing pro-nodulation signalling activity.

text: To investigate whether BTSa and BTSb have distinct roles in nodulation, we expressed BTSa or BTSb under the control of the ubiquitin promoter or their native promoter in the btsa btsb mutant. The expression of BTSa or BTSb in the btsa btsb mutant completely restored its nodulation phenotype (Extended Data Fig. 5a–c). In addition, we generated single btsa and btsb mutants, and nodule numbers and nitrogenase activity were comparable to those in the wild type (Extended Data Fig. 5d–k). These results indicate that BTSa and BTSb have similar roles in regulating nodulation.

text: Since AtBTS has iron-sensing functionality in Arabidopsis54,57, we therefore sought to determine whether and how soybean BTSa responds to iron in the context of nodulation. BTSa was highly induced by iron deficiency in soybean roots (Fig. 4a). Transgenic hairy roots expressing BTSapro:GUS indicated that BTSa promoter activity was upregulated in vascular tissues and extended into the cortical cells under low-iron conditions (Fig. 4b), confirming that BTSa is responsive to iron deficiency. BTSa has three HHE motifs (HHE, iron-binding motif) and a RING zinc-finger domain (Extended Data Fig. 6a). To test iron-binding capability of the HHE motifs, we expressed a full-length recombinant BTSa or a truncated form containing only the three HHE domains fused to maltose-binding protein (MBP) in E. coli (Extended Data Fig. 6b) and measured iron concentrations56,57 associated with them (Fig. 4c). BTSa can directly bind to iron. Notably, BTSa abundance increased dramatically in planta in the presence of increasing concentrations of iron (Fig. 4d–f). In addition, BTSa abundance decreased in the presence of deferiprone (an Fe chelator)68 but increased in the presence of ferric ammonium citrate when expressed in N. bethamiana leaves (Extended Data Fig. 6c). These results suggest that iron stabilizes BTSa, which is in contrast with Arabidopsis BTS being stabilized by iron deficiency57.
section: BTSa acts as an iron sensor during nodulation
title: The BRUTUS iron sensor and E3 ligase facilitates soybean root nodulation by monoubiquitination of NSP1

text: To test whether BTSa and BTSb contribute to soybean’s response to iron deficiency, we assayed iron-responsive marker genes including FRO2 and IRT1 that herald early responses to iron deficiency in roots. FRO2 and IRT1 were sharply induced in the wild type by iron deficiency, but their induction in the btsa btsb-1 mutant was markedly decreased (Fig. 4g). To test whether BTSa and BTSb have similar roles in responses to iron deficiency, we analysed FRO2 and IRT1 expression in the root of btsa and btsb single mutants. FRO2 and IRT1 were reduced in the btsb mutant, but were comparable to the wild type in the btsa mutant (Fig. 4g), suggesting that BTSb plays a primary role in regulating iron uptake. We next investigated potential roles for BTSa and BTSb in nodulation under low-iron conditions. In contrast to the wild type, in which there was a substantial decrease in nodulation under iron deficiency, nodule numbers and nitrogenase activity remained unchanged in both btsa btsb double mutants under low-iron conditions (Fig. 4h and Extended Data Fig. 6d,e). This suggests that BTSa and BTSb are essential for iron-mediated nodulation. Collectively, these results suggest that BTSa and BTSb together (or alone) function as potential iron sensors that modulate nodulation in response to iron status.
section: BTSa acts as an iron sensor during nodulation
title: The BRUTUS iron sensor and E3 ligase facilitates soybean root nodulation by monoubiquitination of NSP1

text: Since BTSa and BTSb physically interact with NSP1a, we wondered whether these proteins transduce iron signals to trigger nodulation by NSP1a. To test this, we first analysed whether BTS affects NSP1a expression. NSP1a induction after inoculation was unaffected in the btsa btsb-1 mutant under normal conditions but decreased under low-iron conditions (Extended Data Fig. 7a). To elucidate whether and how BTSa affects NSP1a protein stability, we first assayed NSP1a degradation in a cell-free system. Recombinant NSP1a–GST was incubated with total-protein extracts from N. bethamiana leaf cells transiently expressing UBIpro:BTSa–3×HA or an empty vector. NSP1a–GST was degraded much more slowly when incubated with protein extracts containing BTSa–3×HA compared with those of empty vector (Extended Data Fig. 7b,c), suggesting that BTSa enhances the stability of NSP1a–GST in vitro. Second, we assessed the effect of BTSa on NSP1a stability in planta. We co-expressed UBIpro:NSP1a–4×MYC with UBIpro:BTSa–3×HA or the empty vector in N. bethamiana leaves. NSP1a–4×MYC accumulated more in leaves co-expressing UBIpro:BTSa–3×HA than those of the empty vector (Extended Data Fig. 7d,e). Third, we transformed UBIpro:NSP1a–4×MYC into wild-type Wm82 and btsa btsb-1 hairy roots. NSP1a–4×MYC abundance in btsa btsb-1 was lower than that in the wild-type control (Fig. 4j), while transgene NSP1a transcript levels in btsa btsb-1 were indistinguishable from those in the wild-type control (Fig. 4k). Finally, we assayed native NSP1a abundance in roots of wild type and both btsa btsb mutants. NSP1a in btsa btsb mutants decreased compared with the wild type under normal conditions and decreased even further under low-iron conditions (Fig. 4l), indicating that BTSa and BTSb are required for the stability of NSP1a.

text: To confirm whether NSP1 monoubiquitination is conserved, we first aligned NSP1 sequences from soybean with those from the Papilionoideae legumes Medicago (M.) truncatula and Lotus (L.) japonicus. Three lysine residues (K133, K139 and K143) in the N-terminal end are conserved in soybean, M. truncatula and L. japonicus; K398 is conserved in soybean and M. truncatula, while K468 is conserved in soybean and L. japonicus (Extended Data Fig. 9a), suggesting that NSP1 proteins in M. truncatula and L. japonicus are probably monoubiquitinated by BTS E3-ligase activity. Yeast two-hybrid and co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) experiments revealed that MtNSP1 and LjNSP1 can indeed interact with MtBTS and LjBTS, respectively (Fig. 6a,b). In vivo ubiquitination assays showed that both FLAG-tagged MtNSP1 and LjNSP1 were monoubiquitinated by their MtBTS and LjBTS partners, and that mutation of the three conserved K residues in MtNSP1 and LjNSP1 completely blocked monoubiquitination by BTS (Fig. 6c), confirming a conserved role for these lysine residues in N-terminal monoubiquitination of legume NSP1s. To validate the role of MtNSP1 and LjNSP1 monoubiquitination in nodulation, we transformed MtNSP1WT–4×MYC, LjNSP1WT–4×MYC and respective mutant forms MtNSP13KR–4×MYC and LjNSP13KR–4×MYC into wild type and nsp1a-1 hairy roots with constructs driven by the UBI promoter. MtNSP1–4×MYC and LjNSP1–4×MYC completely rescued the nodulation defect of nsp1a-1 to the wild-type level, while MtNSP1a3KR–4×MYC and LjNSP13KR–4×MYC did not complement the nsp1a-1 mutant (Fig. 6d and Extended Data Fig. 10a). These data suggest that BTS-mediated monoubiquitination of NSP1 is conserved in legumes. To confirm the legume-specific role of NSP1 monoubiquitination by BTSa, we performed a monoubiquitination assay of NSP1 using Arabidopsis AtBTS. FLAG-tagged NSP1a was not monoubiquitinated by AtBTSa (Extended Data Fig. 10b), and a Co-IP assay revealed no detectable interaction between NSP1 and AtBTS (Extended Data Fig. 10c).

text: Iron has long been appreciated as crucial for symbiotic nitrogen fixation in legumes because nitrogenase and leghaemoglobin require vast amounts of iron41,42,45,74,75. Nodulation is a prerequisite for the establishment of symbiotic nitrogen fixation. As both the host and partner need iron, we propose that sensing iron status and coordinating iron availability by the host during nodulation under varying iron conditions must be an important strategy for the successful establishment of symbiosis. In this work, we provide evidence that iron availability plays a decisive role in the successful nodulation of soybean. We have identified BTSa as an iron sensor that integrates iron and nodulation signalling pathways upon perception of iron status. Our data support a model in which BTSa senses and transduces the early iron signal to NSP1, which elicits nodulation signalling in inoculated roots to promote nodulation. We observed that symbiotic nodulation exhibits a high dependence on iron. The absence of iron completely inhibited soybean nodule initiation even under low-nitrogen and sufficient light conditions. The existing theory is that nitrogen and light are two strong drivers of legume nodulation and symbiotic nitrogen fixation1,30–33. Our observation that iron deficiency blocks soybean nodulation under the conditions of low nitrogen and sufficient light suggests that iron may be as strong a driver as nitrogen and light availability, a notion supported by observations in Lupinus nodulation42–44. Furthermore, we identified a suitable iron concentration (~40 μM) for soybean nodulation, while excess iron levels (>160 μM) were found to inhibit nodulation due to excessive ROS accumulation and cell toxicity. Different leguminous plants and rhizobia may have different iron requirements. Identification of an ‘iron optimum’ for nodulation may represent a mutual strategy by both plants and rhizobia to adapt to varying levels of iron in natural environments.

text: Altogether, our data suggest that host roots can perceive external variation in iron precisely, to coordinate nodulation signalling pathways, which in turn determines the number of nodules formed and the amount of nitrogen fixed. However, understanding exactly how the host coordinates the establishment of a symbiotic yet energetically demanding relationship with rhizobia based on iron availability during nodulation is still in its infancy. We saw that the essential nodulation regulators NINs were downregulated under low-Fe conditions, whereas their transcriptional activators NSP1 and NSP2 remained unaffected. Legume NSP1 proteins are central transcription factors in nodulation signalling11,12,14, the induction of which also mediates nitrogen and phosphorus exchange between host and symbionts76–78. It is possible that NSP1 proteins are regulated by nutritional signals to enhance transcriptional activation activity and subsequently promote symbiosis. Indeed, we demonstrate that NSP1a is involved in iron-mediated nodulation. First, we found that NSP1a protein stability strongly correlates with levels of external iron, and NSP1a stability was high in the presence of sufficient iron, with significant decreases under low-iron conditions. Second, we showed that the binding activity of NSP1a to NIN1a promoter is affected by iron status, with lower binding activity under low-Fe conditions. Third, and most importantly, the inhibitory effect of low Fe on nodulation is attenuated in nsp1 mutants. These NSP1a-dependent responses indicate that NSP1a is a key node in perceiving and transducing low external iron signals to nodulation in soybean roots.

text: of the molecular mechanisms controlling BTS stability will enable us to better understand the regulatory network of iron-level responses in plants during nodulation and development processes. Thus, our findings lead to a proposed model in which rhizobia induce BTSa/b under sufficient iron condition, with BTSa/b perceiving an early status of iron by binding to iron, leading to the stabilization of NSP1 and transmitting the iron signal to the nodulation signalling pathway. Arabidopsis BTS functions as an E3 ligase, which polyubiquitinates and degrades bHLH105/115 to negatively regulate Fe uptake56,57. In soybean, both BTSa/b and NSP1a are positive regulators of nodulation; 604 it is unlikely that BTSa/b polyubiquitinates and degrades NSP1. Interestingly, we have discovered that soybean BTSa/b, but not AtBTS, physically interact with and monoubiquitinate NSP1a to stabilize NSP1a. We identified three lysine residues in the N terminus of NSP1a as the site for its monoubiquitination. Moreover, our data revealed that rhizobia and iron-induced monoubiquitination of NSP1a by BTSa enhances NSP1a stability and subsequent transcriptional activity on the NIN1a promoter, thereby activating nodulation signalling and promoting nodulation. These results suggest that monoubiquitination of soybean BTSa on NSP1 is a neofunctionalization. The observation that the btsa btsb double mutant did not completely inhibit NIN1a induction by rhizobia and nodulation indicates that other BTSs probably mediate this process. This finding uncovers iron sensing and signal-transduction versatility of BTS across plant taxa to provide advantages in integrating iron status with distinct signalling networks to steer adaptation. Due to the presence of four homologues of BTS in soybean, we cannot rule out the possibility that other soybean BTSs exert their functions by polyubiquitinating and degrading their substrates. Subsequent functional and biochemical analyses of the remaining soybean BTSs will facilitate a comprehensive understanding of the regulatory function of these iron-sensing proteins.
title: The BRUTUS iron sensor and E3 ligase facilitates soybean root nodulation by monoubiquitination of NSP1

text: BTSs exert their function by transducing an iron signal to downstream effectors, such as IMA peptides. LjIMA1 plays a role in nodule iron uptake and regulates the nitrogen–iron balance63. However, the relationship between BTS and IMA in regulating iron uptake during early nodulation is still unclear. Further research elucidating the interaction between IMA and BTS in soybean will enhance our comprehension of iron-signal sensing and cellular iron homeostasis in the establishment of symbiotic relationships. Our work highlights that BTSa/b-mediated signalling is at the centre of the early root responses to low iron and rhizobial-derived signals. Notably, our data show that BTSa does not interact with and monoubiquitinate NSP2a, suggesting that BTSa monoubiquitination of NSP1 is substrate specific. In addition, our results showed that BTS-mediated monoubiquitination of NSP1 is conserved in nodulating legumes. The observations that (1) AtBTS does not interact with and monoubiquitinate NSP1a, (2) only NSP1 proteins in nodulating legumes contain three conserved lysine residues at their N terminus for monoubiquitination, and (3) LjRING, the homologue of BTS, positively regulates nodulation64, support this conclusion. Our study has uncovered a specific mechanism by which the BTS–NSP1 module facilitates the coupling of iron and nodulation signalling pathways to regulate iron homeostasis and nodulation. This mechanism is essential for nutritional nodulation in legumes to adapt to fluctuations in iron levels in the environment. Altogether, our findings help to explain how iron status is sensed in the early stages of nodulation, why iron limitation inhibits nodulation, and why three lysine residues in the N terminus of NSP1 are conserved in legumes. Because NSP1 is a key regulator of symbioses between hosts and nitrogen-fixing bacteria, as well as beneficial mycorrhizal fungi, our findings will help to improve our understanding of the molecular mechanisms that govern the nutritional regulation of symbiotic relationships.
